items.title: Rundot
items.text:
Markdown that runs.

Rundot runs the code blocks in a markdown file, one step at a time.

Write a release checklist, a deploy or a setup guide once, and run it the same way every time.

🌐 rundot.dev · 🚀 Install · 🤖 Prompt for your LLM

items.title: What people use it for
items.text:
• Release checklists - Tag, build, publish, announce. In order, every time.
  • Incident runbooks - The reliable steps for fixing issues, automated.
  • Dev setup - One setup guide that works the same on every machine.
  • Onboarding - Guides new contributors can run, not just read.
  • Deploys - Ask before anything destructive happens.
  • Database migrations - Backups and safety checks built into the steps.
  • Agent procedures - Fixed steps for your LLM to follow.
  • Rare chores - The job you do twice a year and always forget.

items.title: It's just markdown
items.text:
Save this as hello.md:

---
title: Say hello
inputs:
  - name: NAME
    description: Who to say hello to
---

# Say hello

A runbook is just markdown. rundot runs the blocks marked `run`, shows the
`docstring` ones, and leaves everything else alone, like this paragraph.

## Greet

```docstring
Saying hello to <NAME>.
```

```sh run
echo "Hello, <NAME>!"
```

## Count the letters

```python run
import os

name = os.environ["NAME"]
print(f"{name} has {len(name)} letters")
```

Check it, then run it:

rundot check hello.md
rundot hello.md

rundot asks for the inputs, shows the plan, and runs each step in order. A runbook reads like documentation and renders on GitHub, so it's still useful without rundot installed.

items.title: Run it in your browser
items.text:
rundot web hello.md opens the markdown file in your browser.

Fill in the inputs, then press ▶ on each block in turn and watch its output appear under it.

See Run it in your browser.

items.title: Know it works before it runs
items.text:
rundot check catches broken frontmatter, undeclared placeholders, and shell or Python syntax errors, with line numbers.

rundot --dry hello.md prints every command with its inputs filled in, and runs nothing.

Go one step at a time with --step, and see each block's code as it runs with --show-code.

items.title: Pause for the bits only a person can do
items.text:
A confirm block stops the run until someone answers y:

```confirm
Publish the GitHub release notes for v<VERSION>.
```

Inputs can be checked against a pattern or a list of choices. Secrets are hidden as you type them and shown as **** in the output and the transcript.

items.title: Your runbooks, everywhere
items.text:
Keep runbooks you use across projects in ~/runbooks, and run them by name from anywhere:

$ rundot library
library: /home/you/runbooks
rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies

$ cd ~/Projects/website
$ rundot rebuild-frontend

A book runs in the folder you're in, so the same one works in every project. See Your runbook library.

items.title: Agents improvise. Runbooks don't.
items.text:
A runbook gives an agent a fixed set of steps to follow instead of working them out each time. Paste this prompt into your chat, or into your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. It teaches the format and asks the agent to check and dry-run every runbook before running it.

An agent runs a runbook with --no-input --json: nothing waits for an answer, and each event is a line of JSON. When a step needs a person, such as a confirm, the run stops with exit code 3 and says what to do. Once it's done, the agent runs the same command again, and the run carries on from there.

items.title: Also in rundot
items.text:
• Transcripts - Set output_path to keep every command, its output and how the run ended.
  • More than shell - Shell and Python are built in. Other languages can be added as backends.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Install rundot
  • The runbook format: everything a runbook can contain
  • The command line: every command, flag and exit code
  • Run it in your browser: the whole runbook on one page, run a block at a time
  • Your runbook library: runbooks you keep for yourself, and run from anywhere
  • Backends: the languages rundot runs, and adding your own

rundot web opens a runbook in your browser and runs it one block at a time, with the same inputs, secrets, transcript and saved state as rundot run. It works offline, and listens on 127.0.0.1 only.

  • Run it in your browser and rundot web
  • Raw HTML and Mermaid diagrams render as on GitHub
  • --json events include each block's filled-in text

A run that stops part way can now be resumed at the step it stopped in. --no-input and --json let an agent or a CI job run a runbook without anything waiting for an answer, stopping with exit code 3 when a person is needed.

  • Resuming a run
  • --no-input and --json
  • Running from an agent or CI

paulrun was renamed rundot. The package, command, imports, entry point group (rundot.backends) and environment variables (RUNDOT_LIBRARY, RUNDOT_RUNBOOK_DIR) changed name and nothing else did; entries below use the old name.

• paulrun run's output is easier to scan:
    • the overview and how the run finished are in boxes
    • each step is a numbered blue rule, e.g. 1/3 Build
    • each block is a bracket: ┌ with its language and when it started (HH:MM:SS.mmm), each line it printed after │, then └ ✓ exit 0 · 0.4s or └ ✗ exit 3 · 0.4s
    • docstrings are dim, and confirms are in a yellow box
  • A line a block writes to stderr has a red │.
  • Code is hidden unless you pass --show-code. --dry always shows it.
  • The transcript is unchanged.
  • Backends: output takes an optional stderr=True for a stderr line, and stream() passes it when output accepts it. A backend that calls output(line) still works.

• A block's output is fenced off between === LOG: <when it started> === and ========, with the time to the microsecond and a blank line either side, so it can't be mistaken for the block's code or paulrun's own lines. A block that prints nothing gets no LOG section. Under --step, a blank line comes before and after Run this block? too. The transcript is unchanged.
• Add a cool logo to the cli output

• A runbook can set step: true in its frontmatter to always run as if --step was given, asking before each run block. --no-step runs it straight through. check reports a step that isn't true or false.
  • The book picker, paulrun run with no runbook, now takes q to quit, and says so: Run which? (q to quit).
  • A block skipped under --step is now shown, and recorded in the transcript, as skipped rather than skipped (--step), since step: true skips blocks too.

items.title: A runbook library
items.text:
• keep runbooks you use across projects in ~/runbooks, or wherever PAULRUN_LIBRARY says. Then run one by name from anywhere, e.g. paulrun rebuild-frontend. run, check and inputs all take a book's name as well as a path, and a file where you are is always used before a book with the same name. paulrun library lists the books in your library, with each one's title and description. paulrun run, with no runbook, lists them by number and runs the one you pick.

  • A new docs page, Your runbook library, with a worked example of a book that rebuilds a frontend under nvm.

  • Breaking: paulrun go is now paulrun run, and you don't need to type it: paulrun RELEASING.md runs RELEASING.md. Anything after paulrun that isn't a command is a runbook to run, so paulrun go is no longer a command. paulrun on its own still shows help.

  • Breaking: blocks now run in the folder you run paulrun from, not the folder the runbook is in. A relative output_path is now relative to that folder too. A runbook kept at the root of its project, run from there, works as before. One run as paulrun path/to/RUNBOOK.md from another folder now works on that other folder and writes its transcript there. This includes blocks run by external backends, whose cwd is now the folder paulrun was started from.
  • Blocks get PAULRUN_RUNBOOK_DIR, the folder the runbook is in, so a runbook can still use files kept next to it.
  • Running a runbook shows the folder blocks will run in, as directory: straight after the title, so you can check it before answering Start?. --dry shows it too.
  • paulrun library, the book picker and paulrun inputs are in colour in a terminal: names you type are bold cyan, details are dim, and secrets and problems stand out. Piped output has no colour, as before.
  • Inputs can have a default, shown at the prompt and used when you press enter. The environment still comes first. check reports a default that isn't text, doesn't match the input's pattern, or is on a secret.
  • Inputs can have choices: the only values accepted, listed at the prompt. You type the choice itself, and a value from the environment has to be one of them too. check reports choices that aren't a list of text, a choice the pattern refuses, a default that isn't a choice, and choices on a secret.

Initial release. paulrun runs hand-written markdown runbooks.

  • paulrun go runs a runbook's steps in order, streaming each block's output as it's printed and stopping at the first block that fails.
  • run blocks for shell (sh, bash, shell) and Python (python, py), with the python frontmatter key to choose the interpreter.
  • docstring blocks to show notes as the runbook runs, and confirm blocks to pause for steps done by hand.
  • input blocks to ask for a value part way through a run, once it exists: a pull request number from a step done by hand, or a one-time code that expires in seconds.
  • Inputs, collected from the environment or by asking, with an optional pattern to check them against. Plain inputs fill in <NAME> placeholders; secrets are hidden as you type them and replaced with **** everywhere paulrun shows or records them.
  • paulrun go --dry to see every block with its inputs filled in, without running anything.
  • paulrun go --step to run, skip or quit at each block.
  • Transcripts: with output_path set, every run is added to a plain record of what ran, what it printed and how it finished.
  • Ctrl-C stops a run cleanly, letting a running block stop and recording how far the run got.
  • paulrun check to find problems before running anything: missing or malformed frontmatter, undeclared placeholders, secrets used as placeholders, blocks outside a step, and shell and Python syntax errors, with shellcheck warnings when it's installed.
  • paulrun inputs to list the inputs a runbook needs, and paulrun backends to list the languages paulrun can run.
  • Backends for other languages can be added by any package, through the paulrun.backends entry point group.

items.title: 🔌 Backends
items.text:
A backend runs run blocks for one or more languages. rundot comes with two, for shell and Python, and other languages can be added by any package.

Run rundot backends to see which backends are installed, the languages each one runs, and the package it comes from:

python  python, py       rundot.backends.python:PythonBackend (rundot 0.2.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  rundot.backends.shell:ShellBackend (rundot 0.2.0)

items.title: Built-in backends
items.text: Backend Languages Needs See shell sh, bash, shell bash Shell blocks python python, py nothing extra Python blocks

items.title: Writing a backend
items.text:
A backend is a plain class with a name, the languages it runs, and two methods: validate() checks a block, and run() runs it. It doesn't need a base class, only to match this protocol from rundot.backends:

class Backend(Protocol):
    """Runs `run` blocks for one or more languages.

    Backends are classes registered under the `rundot.backends` entry point group. Each is created
    once, with no arguments, when backends are loaded.
    """

    # Read-only, so a backend can set them as plain class attributes.
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    @property
    def languages(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        """The fence languages this backend runs, e.g. ("sh", "bash")."""

    def validate(self, code: str) -> list[Problem]:
        """Return the problems found in a block, without running it. An empty list means it's fine.

        code is the block as written, so it can contain <NAME> placeholders. Replacing them with
        something this language accepts is up to the backend. Any error stops the runbook running;
        warnings are only reported.
        """

    def run(
        self,
        code: str,
        *,
        frontmatter: Mapping[str, Any],
        env: Mapping[str, str],
        cwd: Path,
        output: Output,
    ) -> int:
        """Run a block and return its exit code, where 0 means it succeeded.

        Call output with each line the block prints, without its newline, as soon as it's printed, and
        stderr=True for a line it wrote to stderr.
        Don't print anything directly; rundot owns the terminal. frontmatter is the runbook's
        frontmatter, read-only. env is the block's complete environment and cwd is where it runs.
        """

Everything a backend needs is in rundot.backends (Problem, Output, stream and Interrupted) and rundot.inputs (PLACEHOLDER).

items.title: validate()
items.text:
rundot check and rundot run call validate() on every block before anything runs. It returns a list of Problems:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Problem:
    """Something a backend found wrong with a block."""

    message: str
    line: int | None = None  # line in the block, counting its first line as 1; None if it's about the whole block
    warning: bool = False  # warnings are reported but don't stop the runbook running
  • Lines count from the block's first line, as 1. rundot turns them into lines in the runbook.
  • An error stops the run; a warning is only shown.

  • The code still has its <NAME> placeholders. Swap each for something your language accepts before checking it. The built-in backends use the bare name:

    from rundot.inputs import PLACEHOLDER

script = PLACEHOLDER.sub(lambda match: match.group(1), code)

  • Check that what run() needs is installed, so a missing tool is reported before anything runs.

items.title: run()
items.text:
run() gets:

  • code: the block with its placeholders filled in. Secrets are only in env.
  • frontmatter: the runbook's frontmatter, read-only, for settings of your own.
  • env: the block's complete environment. Pass it on as it is.
  • cwd: where the block runs, the folder rundot was started from.
  • output: call it with each line the block prints, as it's printed. Pass stderr=True for a line the block wrote to stderr, and rundot marks it with a red │. output(line) alone is fine too: the line is shown like stdout.

It returns the block's exit code. A backend never prints: rundot shows each line, masks secrets and records the transcript.

items.title: stream()
items.text:
Most backends run a command, and stream() does all of that for you:

def stream(command: Sequence[str], *, env: Mapping[str, str], cwd: Path, output: Callable[..., None]) -> int:

It runs command, passes each line to output as it's printed, and returns the exit code. The built-in backends use it, because it gets the details right:

  • stderr is marked. Each line the command writes to stderr goes to output with stderr=True. stdout and stderr are read separately, so two lines written to them at almost the same moment can arrive in either order. Given an output that only takes the line, stream() merges them instead, in the order they were printed.
  • The command shares rundot's terminal, so it can still ask for a password.
  • Ctrl-C works. The first press lets the command stop by itself; a second kills it and everything it started. Then stream() raises Interrupted with the exit code.

A backend that doesn't use stream() should also raise Interrupted(exit_code) once its block has stopped after Ctrl-C.

items.title: Shipping your own backend
items.text:
Anyone can publish a backend in their own package, and once it's installed alongside rundot, it loads like a built-in one. Here's a complete backend for Node.js, in a package called rundot-node:

rundot-node/
  pyproject.toml
  rundot_node/
    __init__.py

rundot_node/__init__.py:

import re
import shutil
import subprocess
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from rundot.backends import Problem, stream
from rundot.inputs import PLACEHOLDER


class NodeBackend:
    """Runs each block as a Node.js script."""

    name = "node"
    languages = ("js", "javascript")

    def validate(self, code: str) -> list[Problem]:
        if shutil.which("node") is None:
            return [Problem("node isn't installed")]
        # Swap each placeholder for its bare name, which is a plain identifier, so the code still parses.
        script = PLACEHOLDER.sub(lambda match: match.group(1), code)
        result = subprocess.run(["node", "--check"], input=script, capture_output=True, text=True)
        if result.returncode == 0:
            return []
        # node starts with where the error is, e.g. "[stdin]:3", and says what it is further down.
        where = re.match(r"\[stdin\]:(\d+)", result.stderr)
        errors = [line for line in result.stderr.splitlines() if line.startswith("SyntaxError: ")]
        return [Problem(errors[0] if errors else result.stderr.strip(), line=int(where.group(1)) if where else None)]

    def run(
        self,
        code: str,
        *,
        frontmatter: Mapping[str, Any],
        env: Mapping[str, str],
        cwd: Path,
        output: Callable[[str], None],
    ) -> int:
        return stream(["node", "-e", code], env=env, cwd=cwd, output=output)

pyproject.toml registers it under the rundot.backends entry point group:

[project]
name = "rundot-node"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["rundot>=0.1.0"]

[project.entry-points."rundot.backends"]
node = "rundot_node:NodeBackend"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

Install it alongside rundot:

uv tool install rundot --with rundot-node     # once it's on PyPI
uv tool install rundot --with ./rundot-node   # from a local folder, while you work on it

With pip, install it into rundot's environment. Then rundot backends lists it:

node    js, javascript   rundot_node:NodeBackend (rundot-node 0.1.0)
python  python, py       rundot.backends.python:PythonBackend (rundot 0.2.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  rundot.backends.shell:ShellBackend (rundot 0.2.0)

and runbooks can use it:

---
title: Hello from Node
---

## Say hello

```js run
console.log(`Hello from Node ${process.version}`);
```

To test a backend, call its methods directly: run() with output=lines.append, then check the exit code and lines (or output=lambda line, stderr=False: lines.append((line, stderr)) to check which stream each came from), and validate() on a broken block. See rundot's backend tests.

items.title: Things to know
items.text:
• Each language can only have one backend. If two claim the same language, rundot stops with an error naming both.
  • Frontmatter keys of your own get a check warning, since check only knows rundot's keys. It doesn't stop a run.

items.title: Adding a backend to rundot
items.text:
A backend for a widely used language can ship with rundot itself. It's the same code, in a different place:

  1. rundot/backends/<name>.py, implementing the protocol. shell.py and python.py are good models.

  2. One entry point line in rundot's pyproject.toml, next to the built-in ones:

    [project.entry-points."rundot.backends"]
shell = "rundot.backends.shell:ShellBackend"
python = "rundot.backends.python:PythonBackend"

    Then run make install, and uv run rundot backends should list it.

  3. tests/backends/test_<name>.py, which really runs blocks in tmp_path, skipped if the language isn't installed, e.g. pytest.mark.skipif(shutil.which("ruby") is None, reason="ruby isn't installed"). If GitHub's ubuntu-latest doesn't have the language, add a step to .github/workflows/ci.yml that installs it.

  4. A row in Built-in backends, and a section in the runbook format on how its blocks run.
  5. A CHANGELOG entry, in both CHANGELOG.md and docs/CHANGELOG.md.

CONTRIBUTING.md has the rest: setting up, and what to run before opening a pull request.

items.title: 📟 Command line
items.text:
rundot RUNBOOK [--dry] [--step | --no-step] [--show-code]      # run a runbook
rundot run RUNBOOK [--dry] [--step | --no-step] [--show-code]  # the same, in full
rundot web [RUNBOOK] [--port N] [--no-browser]                 # run a runbook in the browser
rundot check RUNBOOK                                           # find problems without running anything
rundot inputs RUNBOOK                                          # list the inputs a runbook needs
rundot library                                                 # list the books in your runbook library
rundot backends                                                # list the languages rundot can run
rundot --version

rundot on its own shows this list.

items.title: Naming a runbook
items.text:
RUNBOOK is a file, or the name of a book in your runbook library:

rundot RELEASING.md        # the file RELEASING.md, here
rundot rebuild-frontend    # the book rebuild-frontend.md, in your library
  1. If RUNBOOK is a file that exists, that's the runbook, so a file is never hidden by a book with the same name.
  2. Otherwise, if it has no /, it's the book <name>.md in your library. The .md is optional.
  3. Otherwise it's a usage error, which names both places rundot looked:
Error: Invalid value for 'RUNBOOK': no runbook 'rebuild-frontend': no such file here, and no rebuild-frontend.md in the library at /home/you/runbooks

items.title: rundot run
items.text:
Runs a runbook, step by step.

rundot RELEASING.md

You don't need to type run: anything after rundot that isn't a command is a runbook. Options go before or after it, so rundot RELEASING.md --dry is the same as rundot --dry RELEASING.md. Use rundot run check to run a book called check.md, since rundot check is the command.

  1. Checks the runbook, as rundot check does. Errors stop it here.
  2. Asks whether to resume, if the last run of this runbook in this directory stopped part way. See Resuming a run.
  3. Collects the inputs. See Inputs.
  4. Shows the plan and asks Start? [y/N].
  5. Runs each step in order, streaming each block's output as it's printed. Each block shows its language and when it started, then what it printed, then its exit code and how long it took. A line it wrote to stderr has a red │.
VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
╭─ Release my-package ─────────────────────╮
│ directory  /home/you/Projects/my-package │
│ inputs     VERSION=1.2.0                 │
│ steps      1. Run the tests              │
│            2. Tag the release            │
│            3. Publish on GitHub          │
│ blocks     2 run blocks                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────╯
Start? [y/N] y

1/3  Run the tests ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh · 10:02:13.482
  │ ...
  └ ✓ exit 0 · 4.2s

2/3  Tag the release ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh · 10:02:17.705
  └ ✓ exit 0 · 0.1s

3/3  Publish on GitHub ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
╭─ confirm ───────────────────────────────╮
│ Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0. │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────╯
Continue? [y/N] y

╭───────────────────────╮
│ ✓ finished ok · 12.8s │
╰───────────────────────╯
transcript: logs/release-1.2.0.md

directory is where blocks will run. See Where blocks run.

The run stops at the first block that fails:

1/1  Build ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh · 10:02:13.482
  │ Building
  │ make: *** [build] Error 2
  └ ✗ exit 2 · 0.0s

╭─────────────────────────────────────╮
│ ✗ failed at "Build" (exit 2) · 0.0s │
╰─────────────────────────────────────╯

Only y answers Start? and Continue? with yes. Anything else, including enter, ends the run as aborted.

items.title: --show-code
items.text:
Shows each block's code above what it printed:

  ┌ sh · 10:02:13.482
  │ echo "Building"
  ├ output
  │ Building
  └ ✓ exit 0 · 0.0s

--dry always shows the code.

items.title: Picking a book
items.text:
With no runbook, rundot run asks which book from your library to run:

$ rundot run
  1. rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
  2. update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies
Run which? (q to quit) 1

Answer with a number. --dry and --step work too. Answer q, or press enter, to stop without running anything.

items.title: --dry
items.text:
Shows what the runbook would do, without running anything.

rundot --dry RELEASING.md
  • Every block is shown with its inputs filled in.
  • There's no Start?, confirm blocks don't wait, and no transcript is written.
  • Secrets and input blocks aren't asked for.
VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
╭─ Release my-package ─────────────────────╮
│ directory  /home/you/Projects/my-package │
│ inputs     VERSION=1.2.0                 │
│ steps      1. Run the tests              │
│            2. Tag the release            │
│            3. Publish on GitHub          │
│ blocks     2 run blocks                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────╯
dry run: nothing will be run

1/3  Run the tests ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh
  │ make test
  └ not run

2/3  Tag the release ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh
  │ git tag 1.2.0
  └ not run

3/3  Publish on GitHub ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
╭─ confirm ───────────────────────────────╮
│ Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0. │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────╯

╭──────────────────────────╮
│ dry run, nothing was run │
╰──────────────────────────╯

items.title: --step
items.text:
Asks before running each run block.

rundot --step RELEASING.md

1/2  Build ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh · 10:02:13.482
  ├ Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit y
  │ Building
  └ ✓ exit 0 · 0.0s

2/2  Publish ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ┌ sh · 10:02:13.486
  ├ Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit s
  └ ↷ skipped

╭──────────────────────╮
│ ✓ finished ok · 0.0s │
╰──────────────────────╯

y runs the block, s skips it, and q ends the run as aborted. The code isn't shown unless you add --show-code. With --dry, --step does nothing, since nothing runs.

A runbook that should always be run this way can set step: true in its frontmatter, so you don't need to remember --step. To run one of those straight through, pass --no-step.

items.title: Pressing Ctrl-C
items.text:
• A running block gets the Ctrl-C too, and rundot waits for it to stop.
  • If a block ignores it, press Ctrl-C again to stop the block and everything it started.
  • The run ends as ✗ interrupted at "<step>".

items.title: Resuming a run
items.text:
A run that stops part way, because a block failed, a confirm was answered no or you pressed Ctrl-C, can be picked up at the step it stopped in. Fix what went wrong, run the same command again, and answer r:

$ rundot RELEASING.md
Last run stopped at 4/5 Publish: failed (exit 1), 2026-11-13 14:02.
[r]esume / [s]tart over / [q]uit: r
PUBLISH_TOKEN (Token for the package index):
╭─ Release my-package ────────────────────────╮
│ directory  /home/you/Projects/my-package    │
│ resuming   4/5 Publish                      │
│ inputs     VERSION=1.2.0 PUBLISH_TOKEN=**** │
│ steps      1. Run the tests       done      │
│            2. Bump the version    done      │
│            3. Tag and push        done      │
│            4. Publish                       │
│            5. Announce                      │
│ blocks     2 run blocks                     │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────╯
Start? [y/N] y

4/5  Publish ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  • r resumes: the steps already done are skipped, and the step it stopped in runs again from its start. Plain inputs are kept from the last run, but secrets are asked for again.
  • s starts over from the first step, and forgets the stopped run.
  • q, or Ctrl-C, runs nothing and keeps the stopped run for next time. rundot exits 1.

If a step the last run did has changed since, or the step it resumes at has a new name, rundot warns before asking, e.g. RELEASING.md has changed since that run: "Tag and push" is different. A runbook that now has fewer steps can't be resumed, so it starts over and says so. A stopped run is only ever resumed in the directory it ran in. See Resuming a run for what's kept, and where.

items.title: --resume and --restart
items.text: --resume resumes without asking. It's an error, exit 1, if there's nothing to resume. --restart forgets any stopped run and starts from the first step. They can't be used together, or with --dry, which never reads or changes a stopped run.

items.title: --no-input
items.text:
rundot never asks anything, so an agent or a CI job can run a runbook:

VERSION=1.2.0 rundot RELEASING.md --no-input
What rundot would ask With --no-input Resume, start over or quit Resumes, and prints resuming at 4/5 Publish. --restart starts over instead. A frontmatter input The environment, then the stopped run, then its default. If any inputs are still missing, the run fails before anything runs and names every one: missing inputs: VERSION, BRANCH. Set them in the environment. Exit 1. Start? [y/N] Yes. Run this block? Never asked: stepping is off, even with step: true in the runbook. A confirm block Stops the run: needs human input: Publish the GitHub release notes for v1.2.0. Run again once it's done. Exit 3. The next run carries on after the confirm, as if it had been answered yes. An input block The environment, then the stopped run, then its default. Otherwise it stops the run: needs human input: set PR (The number GitHub gave the pull request) and run again. Exit 3. The next run, with it set, carries on from that block.

A value from the environment or the stopped run that doesn't fit the input's pattern or choices fails, exit 1.

RUNDOT_NO_INPUT=1 does the same as --no-input, for CI jobs that run rundot through scripts you don't control. Any other value, including an empty one, leaves it off.

--no-input can't be used with --step or --dry, or without a runbook, since picking a book is asking. Those are usage errors, exit 2, whether it's turned on by the flag or the variable.

items.title: --json
items.text:
Prints each of the run's events as one line of JSON on stdout, as it happens, so an agent can follow a run without reading boxes. --json implies --no-input, since a prompt would put text that isn't JSON on stdout.

{"event": "overview", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:03.104+00:00", "title": "Release my-package", "directory": "/home/you/Projects/my-package", "inputs": {"VERSION": "1.2.0", "PUBLISH_TOKEN": "****"}, "steps": ["Run the tests", "Bump the version", "Tag and push", "Publish", "Announce"], "resuming_at": 3, "blocks": {"41": "uv publish --token \"$PUBLISH_TOKEN\"\n", "50": "Publish the GitHub release notes for v1.2.0.\n"}}
{"event": "step_started", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:03.106+00:00", "number": 4, "name": "Publish"}
{"event": "block_started", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:03.106+00:00", "line": 41, "language": "sh", "code": "uv publish --token \"$PUBLISH_TOKEN\"\n"}
{"event": "output", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:03.512+00:00", "text": "Uploading rundot-0.7.0.whl", "stderr": false}
{"event": "block_finished", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:04.307+00:00", "line": 41, "exit_code": 0, "duration": 1.201}
{"event": "step_started", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:04.308+00:00", "number": 5, "name": "Announce"}
{"event": "confirm", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:04.308+00:00", "line": 50, "text": "Publish the GitHub release notes for v1.2.0.\n"}
{"event": "run_finished", "at": "2026-11-13T14:20:04.309+00:00", "status": "needs_human_input", "step": "Announce", "exit_code": null, "duration": 1.205, "message": "Publish the GitHub release notes for v1.2.0. Run again once it's done."}

stdout is JSON lines only. Everything else rundot says, such as check problems, resuming at, missing inputs and needs human input, goes to stderr as text. The transcript is written as usual.

Every object has event and at, when it happened, in ISO 8601 with milliseconds. Secrets are ****, as everywhere else.

event From Fields besides event and at overview Overview title, directory, inputs, steps, resuming_at (the index of the step a resumed run starts at, or null), blocks (each block's text by line, with plain inputs filled in as at the start) step_started StepStarted number (from 1), name docstring Docstring line, text confirm Confirm line, text confirm_answered ConfirmAnswered line, yes input_block InputBlock line, name, description input_collected InputCollected line, name, value, blocks (each later block's text by line, filled in with a plain value; empty for a secret) block_started BlockStarted line, language, code block_skipped BlockSkipped line output OutputLine text, stderr block_finished BlockFinished line, exit_code, duration (seconds) run_finished RunFinished status, step (its name, or null), exit_code, duration, message (what a person has to do, or null)
  • line is the block's line in the runbook, so an agent can point at it.
  • status is ok, failed, aborted, interrupted or needs_human_input.
  • A field may be added in a later version. One is never removed or renamed without a major version.

--json can't be used with --dry or --step, or without a runbook. Those are usage errors, exit 2.

items.title: --web
items.text: rundot run RUNBOOK --web, and rundot RUNBOOK --web, do the same as rundot web RUNBOOK. With no runbook, the browser opens on the library, not the picker. --web can't be used with --dry, --step, --no-step, --show-code, --no-input, --json, --resume or --restart: the page asks, runs one block at a time, and resumes or starts over from its own buttons. Those are usage errors, exit 2.

items.title: rundot web
items.text:
Opens a runbook in the browser and runs it there, one block at a time. See Run it in your browser for how the page works.

rundot web RELEASING.md

rundot web: http://127.0.0.1:51234/book/RELEASING?t=V8m0kq3s…
Ctrl-C to stop

RUNBOOK is a file or a book in your library, as for rundot run. It's checked first, and errors stop it, exit 1. With no RUNBOOK, the browser opens on your library.

  • / is always the library. Each book is at /book/<name>.
  • A runbook opened by its path is at /book/<file name>, or /book/<file name>-2, -3 and so on if a book in your library has the same name.
  • The URL rundot prints goes straight to the runbook you named. Its ?t= is a one-time token: the first visit swaps it for a cookie, and the server refuses anything without it. See Security.

The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It runs until you press Ctrl-C, which saves a running run as interrupted and exits 130.

items.title: --port
items.text: --port picks the port to listen on, e.g. --port 8000. By default, rundot picks any free one. A port that's in use is an error, exit 1.

items.title: --no-browser
items.text: --no-browser prints the URL, with its token, without opening the browser.

items.title: rundot check
items.text:
Finds problems in a runbook without running anything.

rundot check RELEASING.md

RELEASING.md: ok

Each problem is shown with its line, so your editor can jump to it:

broken.md:6: error: input VERSION is declared twice (first on line 4)
broken.md:8: warning: input BRANCH is never used
broken.md:12: error: run blocks must be inside a step (a ## heading)
broken.md:19: error: <TAG> isn't a declared input
broken.md:21: error: syntax error near unexpected token `fi'

4 errors, 1 warning

Errors stop the runbook running:

  • a missing title, or a frontmatter value of the wrong type
  • an input without a name or description, a name that isn't UPPER_SNAKE_CASE or is declared twice, or a pattern that isn't a valid regular expression
  • a default or choices that can't work. See Defaults and Choices.
  • a placeholder that isn't a declared input, or a secret used as a placeholder
  • an input block that isn't valid YAML, or is used before it's asked for
  • a block before the first ## heading
  • a run block in a language no backend runs, or a python command that isn't installed
  • a syntax error in a shell or Python block

Warnings don't:

  • a frontmatter or input key rundot doesn't know, often a typo
  • an input nothing uses
  • a Python SyntaxWarning, and shellcheck findings if it's installed

items.title: rundot inputs
items.text:
Lists the inputs a runbook needs, so you know what to have ready.

rundot inputs PUBLISHING.md

VERSION  The version being released, e.g. 1.2.0
         pattern: ^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$
BRANCH   The branch to release from
         default: main
PR       The number GitHub gave the pull request
         pattern: ^\d+$
         asked in "Open the pull request"
OTP      The code from your authenticator app
         pattern: ^\d{6}$
         secret
         asked in "Publish"

Inputs from input blocks come last, with the step that asks for them. Frontmatter inputs are listed even if the rest of the runbook is broken.

items.title: rundot library
items.text:
Lists the books in your runbook library, with each one's title and description.

$ rundot library
library: /home/you/runbooks
rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
                     Clean install the frontend's dependencies, then rebuild it.
update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies

A book whose frontmatter can't be read is still listed, with why.

items.title: rundot backends
items.text:
Lists the languages rundot can run, and the package each comes from.

$ rundot backends
python  python, py       rundot.backends.python:PythonBackend (rundot 0.2.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  rundot.backends.shell:ShellBackend (rundot 0.2.0)

items.title: Running from an agent or CI
items.text:
Run with --no-input --json, and set the runbook's inputs in the environment:

VERSION=1.2.0 rundot RELEASING.md --no-input --json

Nothing waits for an answer. Read stdout line by line for what's happening, and the exit code for how it ended:

  • 0: the run finished.
  • 1: something failed. stderr says what, e.g. a failed block or missing inputs. Fix it and run the same command again: the run resumes at the step that failed.
  • 3: a person has to do something, such as a confirm step or setting an input. Hand them the needs human input: line from stderr, which is also message in the last JSON line. Once they've done it, run the same command again, and the run carries on from there.

--restart starts from the first step instead of resuming.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text: Code Meaning 0 The run finished, or check found no errors. 1 A block failed, the run was aborted or interrupted, check found errors, inputs were missing under --no-input, or the runbook couldn't be read. Ctrl-C under rundot run exits 1. 2 The command was used wrongly, e.g. a runbook that doesn't exist, or flags that can't be used together, such as --dry with --resume. 3 Human input is needed: the run stopped under --no-input at a confirm, or at an input block with no value. Run again once it's done. 130 Ctrl-C stopped rundot web.

items.title: 🚀 Install
items.text: rundot is a command-line tool, so install it on its own rather than into a project:

items.title: uv
items.text: uv tool install rundot

items.title: pip
items.text:
pip install rundot

Once installed, check it's working:

> rundot --version
rundot, version 0.2.0

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Python 3.12 or later.
  • macOS or Linux. Windows isn't supported.
  • bash, which runs shell blocks. It's on macOS and almost every Linux system already.

items.title: Optional: shellcheck
items.text:
If shellcheck is installed, rundot check uses it to warn about common mistakes in shell blocks, such as an unquoted variable. Without it, shell blocks are still checked for syntax errors.

brew install shellcheck      # macOS
sudo apt install shellcheck  # Debian and Ubuntu

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• The runbook format to write your first runbook
  • The command line to see everything rundot can do

items.title: 📚 Your runbook library
items.text:
Some runbooks belong to a project, like the RELEASING.md at the root of a package. Others are jobs you do the same way across every project. Those go in your runbook library.

Your library is a directory of markdown files that rundot can execute, and we call these books. Move a book there once, and run it by name from wherever you are:

cd ~/Projects/website
rundot rebuild-frontend

items.title: Where your library is
items.text:
Your library is ~/runbooks. Every .md file directly inside it is a book, named after its file: ~/runbooks/rebuild-frontend.md is the book rebuild-frontend. Folders and other files in it aren't books, so ~/runbooks/logs/ is a fine place for transcripts.

To keep it somewhere else, set RUNDOT_LIBRARY:

export RUNDOT_LIBRARY=~/work-runbooks

items.title: Running a book
items.text:
rundot rebuild-frontend        # run it
rundot --dry rebuild-frontend  # see what it would do first
rundot check rebuild-frontend  # find problems in it

A file in the current directory always comes first, so a book never hides a runbook in your project. See Naming a runbook.

A book runs in the directory you're in, not in your library, and rundot shows it as directory before anything runs. See Where blocks run.

items.title: Finding a book
items.text:
rundot library lists your books, with each one's title and description:

$ rundot library
library: /home/you/runbooks
rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
                     Clean install the frontend's dependencies under nvm, then rebuild it.
update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies

Or run rundot run with no runbook, and pick one by number:

$ rundot run
  1. rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
  2. update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies
Run which? (q to quit) 1

items.title: Example: rebuilding a frontend under nvm
items.text:
This book clean-installs a frontend's dependencies with the Node version the project asks for, then rebuilds it. Save it as ~/runbooks/rebuild-frontend.md, and run it from the project's root.

---
title: Rebuild the frontend
description: Clean install the frontend's dependencies under nvm, then rebuild it.
inputs:
  - name: FE_SET
    description: Which frontend set to rebuild
    choices: [main, admin, all]
    default: main
---

# Rebuild the frontend

Run this from the project's root. It uses the Node version in
`frontend/.nvmrc`, and needs [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm).

## Check the project

```sh run
test -f frontend/.nvmrc || { echo "No frontend/.nvmrc here; run this from the project's root."; exit 1; }
```

## Clean install and rebuild

nvm is a shell function your profile loads, so the block loads it itself.
Everything that needs the project's Node is in this one block, since a later
block would be back on your default Node.

```sh run
source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"
cd frontend
nvm install
nvm use
rm -rf node_modules
npm ci
npm run build -- --set=<FE_SET>
```

Two things in it apply to any book:

  • Load what your profile sets up. rundot runs shell blocks with a plain bash, which doesn't read your profile, so shell functions like nvm, pyenv and rbenv aren't there. source them in the block.
  • Keep one environment in one block. A cd or nvm use is gone by the next block, and that fails quietly: the next block just runs with your default Node. So everything that needs the project's Node goes in the block with nvm use.

items.title: 📜 Runbook format
items.text:
A runbook is a markdown file. Frontmatter at the top sets it up, each ## heading is a step, and code blocks marked for rundot are shown, paused on, or run. Everything else is documentation.

Run rundot check on a runbook to find anything wrong with it.

items.title: Frontmatter
items.text:
YAML between --- lines at the top of the file:

---
title: Release my-package                    # required
description: Release a new version.          # optional
output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md       # optional
python: uv run python                        # optional
step: true                                   # optional, default false
inputs:                                      # optional
  - name: VERSION                            # required
    description: The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0   # required
    pattern: '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'               # optional
  - name: PUBLISH_TOKEN
    description: Token for the package index
    secret: true                             # optional, default false
---
Key What it does title The runbook's name, shown when it runs. Required. description What it's for, shown by rundot library. output_path Where to keep a transcript of each run. python The command that runs Python blocks. step true to ask before each run block, as --step does, without having to pass it. --no-step turns it off for one run. inputs Values to ask for. See Inputs.

Any other key is a check warning, so a typo like ouput_path gets noticed.

items.title: Inputs
items.text:
Values a runbook needs each time it runs, such as the version being released.

Key What it does name Required, in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, e.g. VERSION. description Required. Shown when rundot asks for it. pattern A regular expression the whole value must match, e.g. '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'. secret true for passwords and tokens. See Secrets. default Used if you press enter. See Defaults. choices The only values accepted. See Choices.

rundot collects every input before the first step:

  1. If an environment variable with the input's name is set, it's used: VERSION=1.2.0 rundot RELEASING.md doesn't ask. An empty variable counts as not set.
  2. Otherwise rundot asks for it.

A typed answer that doesn't fit the input's pattern or choices is asked for again. A value from the environment that doesn't fit stops rundot before anything runs.

items.title: Using inputs
items.text:
Every input is an environment variable in every run block: $VERSION in shell, os.environ["VERSION"] in Python.

An input that isn't secret can also be written as a placeholder, <VERSION>, in run, docstring and confirm blocks and in output_path. rundot fills it in. The rest of the runbook is never changed.

A placeholder that isn't a declared input is a check error, and an input nothing uses, as <VERSION> or $VERSION, is a warning.

Placeholders are filled in as plain text

If someone enters 1.2.0; rm -rf ~ for <VERSION>, that's what the block runs. Give inputs used in commands a pattern.

items.title: Defaults
items.text:
inputs:
  - name: BRANCH
    description: The branch to release from
    default: main

BRANCH (The branch to release from) [main]:

Pressing enter takes main. The environment still comes first, and a default must still match the input's pattern.

Quote a default YAML would read as something other than text, such as default: '1.10', which would otherwise be the number 1.1. A secret can't have a default.

items.title: Choices
items.text:
inputs:
  - name: FE_SET
    description: Which frontend set to rebuild
    choices: [comms, billing, all]
    default: comms

FE_SET (Which frontend set to rebuild) [comms] (comms, billing, all): everything
FE_SET must be one of: comms, billing, all

Type the choice itself, not its number. Choices are compared exactly, so Comms isn't comms. A default must be one of the choices, every choice must match the pattern if there is one, and a secret can't have choices.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
An input with secret: true is never shown or saved:

  • Its prompt hides what's typed.
  • It's never a placeholder. Read it as $PUBLISH_TOKEN; writing <PUBLISH_TOKEN> is a check error.
  • Its value is shown as **** in block output and the transcript.
  • rundot --dry doesn't ask for it.
uv publish --token "$PUBLISH_TOKEN"

Note

rundot spots a secret by its exact value, one line at a time. A command that encodes it, or splits it across lines, can still reveal it. Pass secrets to commands rather than printing them.

items.title: Input blocks
items.text:
Some values only exist part way through a run, like the number GitHub gives a pull request you've just opened. An input block asks for one when the run reaches it:

## Open the pull request

```confirm
Open a pull request for <VERSION> on GitHub.
```

```input
name: PR
description: The number GitHub gave the pull request
pattern: '^\d+$'
```

```sh run
gh pr merge <PR>
```

It takes the same keys as a frontmatter input, and works the same from then on.

  • Using it before the block, or in output_path, is a check error.
  • rundot --dry doesn't ask for it, and shows <PR> as written.

A one-time code is a good use of a secret input block:

```input
name: OTP
description: The code from your authenticator app
pattern: '^\d{6}$'
secret: true
```

```sh run
npm publish --otp "$OTP"
```

items.title: Steps
items.text:
Each ## heading starts a step, named by its text. ### and smaller headings are just text inside the step.

A block before the first ## heading is a check error.

items.title: Blocks
items.text:
The first word of a code block's opening line is its language. A second word of run makes rundot run it.

Block What rundot does ```docstring Shows the text. ```confirm Shows the text and waits for y. Any other answer ends the run. ```input Asks for an input. See Input blocks. ```sh run Runs it. See Run blocks. ```mermaid Nothing. rundot web draws it as a diagram. See Diagrams. Anything else, e.g. ```sh Nothing. It's documentation.

So a plain ```sh block shows a command without rundot running it.

```docstring
Releasing <VERSION>. This takes a few minutes.
```

```confirm
Create a GitHub release from tag <VERSION>, then come back here.
```

items.title: Run blocks
items.text:
rundot shows each block's output as it's printed. Exit code 0 carries on; anything else stops the run.

Every block runs with rundot's environment and every input, plus:

  • RUNDOT_RUNBOOK_DIR, the folder the runbook is in
  • PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, so Python output isn't held back
  • PAGER=cat and GIT_PAGER=cat, so nothing waits in a pager

Run rundot backends to see which languages you can use, or add your own with backends.

items.title: Where blocks run
items.text:
Blocks run in the folder you run rundot from, not the runbook's folder. So one runbook can work on whichever project you're in:

cd ~/Projects/website
rundot ~/runbooks/update-deps.md

Use $RUNDOT_RUNBOOK_DIR for files kept next to the runbook:

cp "$RUNDOT_RUNBOOK_DIR/templates/pull-request.md" .github/

Each block is its own process, so a cd or export is gone by the next block. Keep commands that need them together.

items.title: Shell blocks
items.text: sh, bash or shell. Each block is one bash script that stops at the first failing command, as if it began with set -eo pipefail. check finds syntax errors, and shellcheck warnings if it's installed.

items.title: Python blocks
items.text:
python or py. Each block is its own script, run with the Python rundot runs on, so only the standard library is available. To use another interpreter or your project's dependencies, set python:

python: uv run python

check compiles each block with rundot's own Python, so syntax only a newer Python understands isn't caught.

items.title: Blocks that ask questions
items.text: A block can still ask on the terminal, the way git and ssh ask for a password. But output is shown a line at a time, so a question with no newline after it isn't shown until you answer. Use inputs for values instead.

items.title: In the browser
items.text: rundot web shows the whole runbook, not just its blocks.

items.title: Raw HTML
items.text:
HTML in a runbook renders as it does on GitHub. Tags and attributes GitHub allows, such as <details>, <summary>, <kbd> and <img width>, are kept. Everything else is removed, including <script>, <style>, <iframe>, <form>, every on… attribute and any link that isn't http, https, mailto or relative.

<details>
<summary>Why this step exists</summary>

The old release script skipped it, and 1.1.0 shipped without a changelog.

</details>

Images with a relative path are served from the runbook's folder. A path that leaves it isn't served.

items.title: Diagrams
items.text:
A ```mermaid block is drawn as a diagram, as GitHub draws it, with Pele. Pele ships inside rundot, so diagrams draw offline. A diagram Pele can't draw stays as code, with its error under it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Write the runbook] --> B{Does it run?}
  B -- yes --> C[Ship it]
  B -- no --> D[Fix it]
```

rundot run leaves mermaid blocks alone, like any other block it doesn't run.

items.title: Resuming a run
items.text:
A run that stops part way can be resumed at the step it stopped in, so the steps already done aren't run again. See Resuming a run for how to resume one.

  • Where it's kept. rundot notes where each run has got to in $XDG_STATE_HOME/rundot/runs/, or ~/.local/state/rundot/runs/ if that isn't set. Nothing is written to your project. A run is known by its runbook and the directory its blocks run in, so the same runbook run in two projects is resumed separately.
  • When. It's noted as each step starts, so even a run that was killed outright can be resumed. It's deleted when the run finishes ok. --dry never reads or writes it, and a run you decline at Start? leaves the last one as it was.
  • What's kept. Plain input values, from the frontmatter and from input blocks, are kept and used again, after the environment. Secrets are never kept: they're read from the environment or asked for again.
  • Where it resumes. At the start of the step the run stopped in, so a step is always run whole. Its confirm blocks are asked again. The one exception is a run stopped under --no-input at a confirm or an input block, which carries on at that block: the confirm counts as done, and the input is read from the environment.
  • A changed runbook. If a step that's done has changed since, or the step it resumes at has a new name, rundot warns and still offers to resume. If the runbook now has fewer steps, it starts over.

items.title: Transcript
items.text:
Set output_path, and each run is added to the end of that file, so a failed attempt and the rerun that fixed it are both kept:

output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md

A relative path is relative to the folder you run rundot from. Missing folders are created, and --dry runs aren't recorded.

--- rundot RELEASING.md @ 2026-10-12T15:11:27+01:00
--- inputs: VERSION=1.2.0 PUBLISH_TOKEN=****

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
<everything make test printed>
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
confirm: Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0. -> yes

=== Publish to PyPI ===
input: OTP=****
    uv publish --token "$PUBLISH_TOKEN"
skipped

--- finished: ok (3m12s)

The last line says how the run ended:

Last line When --- finished: ok (3m12s) Every step ran. --- finished: failed at "<step>" (exit N) A block exited with N. --- finished: aborted at "<step>" A confirm wasn't answered y, or you quit with --step. --- finished: interrupted at "<step>" You pressed Ctrl-C. --- finished: needs human input at "<step>" Under --no-input, the run reached a confirm, or an input block with no value.

A resumed run has one more line at the top, saying which step it resumed at and which run it resumed:

--- rundot RELEASING.md @ 2026-10-12T15:20:03+01:00
--- resumed at "Publish to PyPI", from the run at 2026-10-12T15:11:27+01:00
--- inputs: VERSION=1.2.0 PUBLISH_TOKEN=****

items.title: Known limits
items.text:
• bash on macOS is version 3.2, which can't spot an unclosed heredoc (cat <<EOF with no EOF).
  • Windows isn't supported.

items.title: 🌐 Run it in your browser
items.text: rundot web opens a runbook in your browser as the whole document, prose and all, and runs it there one block at a time. It runs the runbook the same way rundot run does, with the same inputs, secret masking, confirms, transcript and saved state.

items.title: Starting it
items.text:
rundot web RELEASING.md        # a file
rundot web rebuild-frontend    # a book in your library
rundot RELEASING.md --web      # the same as rundot web RELEASING.md
rundot web                     # your library

RUNBOOK is found as for rundot run. rundot checks it first, and a runbook with errors stops here, as it would under rundot run. Then rundot opens your browser and prints:

rundot web: http://127.0.0.1:51234/book/RELEASING?t=V8m0kq3s…
Ctrl-C to stop

The page stays up until you press Ctrl-C. Blocks run in the folder you started rundot web from. See rundot web for --port and --no-browser.

items.title: The page
items.text:
The runbook's title is at the top, with its description under it, then a form for its inputs. The rest of the runbook follows as it reads on GitHub, and links to these docs and rundot.dev are at the foot of the page.

A secret is a password field:

Fill in the form and press Start. A value that doesn't fit the input's pattern or choices shows why under its field. Once the run starts, the form folds into one line, with secrets as ****:

items.title: Running each block
items.text:
Only the next block's ▶ can be pressed. Blocks before it are done, and blocks after it wait their turn. Press ▶ to run it.

  • What a block prints shows under it, as it's printed. Lines it writes to stderr are red.
  • The block ends with ✓ exit 0 or ✗ exit 1 and how long it took.
  • Each step heading shows n/total, then ✓ or ✗ once the step is done.
  • Placeholders such as <NAME> are filled in once the run starts, in every block, including those the run hasn't reached yet. A value an input block asks for fills in the blocks after it once it's given. Secrets never are.

items.title: Confirms
items.text: A confirm block waits for you to do something by hand. Press Done once you have, or Stop to end the run there.

items.title: Input blocks
items.text: An input block is a field where it sits in the runbook. It's checked against its pattern and choices, as in the terminal:

items.title: When a block fails
items.text:
The run stops at the block that failed, with its output and exit code:

The top of the page says where it stopped:

  • Retry step runs the step again from its start, once you've fixed the problem.
  • Start over forgets the stopped run and goes back to the form.

A run ended with Stop gets the same buttons. When a run finishes, Run again starts a new one.

items.title: Resuming
items.text:
A run stopped in the browser can be resumed with rundot run, and a run stopped with rundot run can be resumed in the browser. Both use the same saved state and write the same transcript.

Opening a runbook whose last run stopped part way shows where it stopped:

  • Resume picks the run up at the start of the step it stopped in. Plain inputs come from the stopped run. Secrets are never saved, so the form asks for them again.
  • Start over forgets the stopped run.

If the runbook has changed since that run, the banner says what changed, as rundot run does.

items.title: The library
items.text: rundot web with no runbook opens on your library. Every page has ← Library at the top, which goes back to it. A runbook you opened by its path is listed first.

items.title: One run at a time
items.text:
Only one book runs at a time, and only the tab that started a run can answer it. Open another book while one is running, or the running book in a second tab, and the page says which one is running. A second tab of the running book replays the run so far and follows it live, but its buttons wait until that run is done, as another book's do.

Reloading the tab that started the run replays the run so far, and it carries on from there. The tab keeps its place through a reload, but not once it's closed. Then Ctrl-C in the terminal stops rundot web and saves the run as interrupted, and the next rundot web can resume it. Duplicating that tab copies its place too, so the copy can answer the run as well.

items.title: Diagrams and HTML
items.text: A ```mermaid block is drawn as a diagram, and raw HTML such as <details> renders as it does on GitHub. See In the browser.

items.title: In a narrow window
items.text: The page fits a window as narrow as a phone's:

items.title: Pressing Ctrl-C
items.text: Press Ctrl-C in the terminal to stop rundot web. A running block gets the Ctrl-C too, and rundot waits for it to stop. The run is saved as interrupted, so it can be resumed, and rundot web exits with code 130. If a block ignores it, press Ctrl-C again to stop waiting.

items.title: Security
items.text:
The page runs commands on your computer, so only you can reach it:

  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 only. There's no option to listen anywhere else.
  • It refuses any request whose Host isn't 127.0.0.1 or localhost on its port, so another website can't reach it through DNS.
  • It refuses any button press that doesn't come from its own pages, by their Origin, so another website open in your browser can't press ▶.
  • The URL rundot prints has a one-time token. The first visit swaps it for a cookie that only this server's pages get (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict), and every request after that needs the cookie. Other programs and users on your computer don't have it.
  • Every page is sent with Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self', so a script that gets into a runbook's HTML can't run.
  • Secret values never reach the browser after you submit them. Output is masked before it's sent, as it is in the terminal and the transcript.

items.title: Offline
items.text: The page's styles, fonts, script and diagram renderer are all inside rundot. Nothing is fetched from the internet, so it works with no network.
